items.name: Readability
items.evidence: Neither language section has any comments, even on the polyglot trick (`#if 0` / `r""" "`), which the conventions ask to be commented. The C bignum loop is unexplained: magic `1000000000ULL` limbs and `cap = n/40 + 10`. Names are single letters: `a`, `b`, `n`, `cap`, `len`.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: C `main` is one ~37-line block that mixes argument parsing, a hand-rolled base-1e9 bignum, printing and freeing. This is more machinery than the task needs. The Python section is clean. No dead code or debug output.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: `calloc` results are never checked. `atol(argv[1])` turns non-numeric input into 0 and prints "0" with exit 0. Negative n silently prints 0 in both languages. A missing argument exits 1 with no message. `(int)(n / 40)` can overflow for huge n. Magic constants: 1e9, 40, 10.

items.name: Boundary and large inputs
items.evidence: Both sides give f(0)=0 and f(1)=1, use iterative arbitrary precision, and match up to n=1000. Missing arg exits 1 in both. But negative n prints `0` instead of an error, and in C non-numeric input (`atol`) prints `0` with exit 0, which is garbage rather than a rejection.

items.name: Exact invocation contract
items.evidence: Works with the plain `gcc file -o cmain` and `python3 file N` commands, no extra flags. The quote tokens in the `#if 0` blocks are balanced for C and form a valid raw string for Python. Only the number goes to stdout. It compiled cleanly under -Wall -Wextra -pedantic, and the hidden test passed.
